blocks.md: This lesson follows **Fallacies and Pitfalls** in *The Agent Harness* (Vol III).

blocks.source: Vol III, The Agent Harness, § Fallacies and Pitfalls
blocks.md: Architectural failures in agent systems rarely stem from exotic distributed bugs; they occur when engineers mistake a convenient implementation mechanism or an agreeable language model for an authoritative supervisory guarantee. The harness must enforce safety, resource bounds, and lifecycle invariants externally, regardless of how cooperative the model appears.

blocks.prompt: Think first: In two or three sentences, explain why Bounded-liability admission matters for the system this section describes.
blocks.md: Compare your answer with the book's claim: A budget is an enforceable ceiling only if each operation is admitted when actual consumption plus outstanding reservations plus its worst-case liability plus a protected finalization reserve fits the allowance in every dimension.

questions.q: The section **Fallacies and Pitfalls** develops one of the chapter's claims. Which one?
options: Supervision needs one authoritative per-trajectory control record, written only by the harness, holding contract, lifecycle state, accounting, grants, current invocations, the operation table, and a live plan.

Operator control takes effect at turn boundaries, so a harness that checks only when a reply ends lets one call postpone a pause by K_max x t_dec, and pause, interrupt, cancel, kill, and budget stop change admission differently.
Cancelling a stream removes the dependence of control latency on output length, and partial or canceled output is quarantined and never dispatched.

A budget is an enforceable ceiling only if each operation is admitted when actual consumption plus outstanding reservations plus its worst-case liability plus a protected finalization reserve fits the allowance in every dimension.
